# 1 Corinthians 9: research notes

**About these notes:** I ran out of search and fetch requests before I could read several sources you listed. I could not reach netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or any Lutheran site. I also found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. Where a Catholic reading appears below, it comes from Protestant commentators describing it, not from Catholic sources themselves. I have only labelled a writer's tradition where the page itself labels it. A few verses are covered under the verse group a commentator discusses them in (vv. 7–12, 13–14, 16–17, 24–25).

---

**Overview**
- Guzik sees Paul's own example as the model for the Corinthians: they should sometimes give up their "right" to eat meat offered to idols, out of love for a weaker believer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/
- Ellicott thinks the end of chapter 8 reminded Paul of another sacrifice he had made, working as a tentmaker instead of taking support. Some people had used that to question his standing as an apostle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm

**v. 1**
- In the better manuscripts "Am I not free?" comes first, which links it more naturally to chapter 8. To have seen Christ was a requirement for being an apostle (Acts 1:21). (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm
- Paul answered to no one but Christ. He saw a real appearance of the risen Jesus, not just a vision. Guzik warns that a vision does not make someone an apostle today, because Paul was also specifically commissioned (Acts 26:12-18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/

**v. 2**
- "Others" probably means teachers who reached Corinth after Paul left and did not accept him. The repeated "in the Lord" shows Paul's conviction that all success comes from Christ. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm
- The Corinthians had seen his work up close, so their doubt was ironic. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/

**v. 3**
- "Defense" and "examine" are courtroom words. Ellicott takes the verse as referring back to vv. 1–2, not forward. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm
- Guzik: Paul writes as if he were on trial. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/

**v. 4**
- The point is the right to eat and drink at the church's expense (Luke 10:7). The plural "we" claims a right shared by all the apostles. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm

**v. 5 (a real dividing line)**
- Traditional Protestant reading: "sister, wife" means a believing wife, who also had a right to support. Peter was married (Matthew 8:14). (Ellicott; Vincent; Barnes) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/9-5.htm
- Matthew Henry argues Paul could have married and claimed support for a family. Apostles travelling with women who were not their wives would have caused scandal. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/9-5.html
- Several Protestant writers use the verse against compulsory clerical celibacy: Clarke, Barnes, Coffman, the Light of Israel commentary, and Guzik on Peter as "first pope." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/9-5.html and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/
- The other reading, as Protestants report it: Ellicott says "Roman divines" took the verse to mean Christian matrons who served the apostles as "sisters." The Pulpit Commentary says Augustine, Tertullian, Ambrose and others read it as "ministering women" (Luke 8:2-3). It also says later scribes altered the text. The Douay-Rheims renders it "a woman, a sister." https://biblehub.com/1_corinthians/9-5.htm and https://www.biblehub.com/catholic/1_corinthians/9-5.htm
- Gill rejects the reading that these were wealthy women providing for the apostles, because it runs against Paul's argument about churches supporting them. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/spa/sag/1-corinthians/9-5.html
- "The Lord's brothers": Ellicott names Joses, Simon and Judas, and James, who later held an apostle's role. He says the "cousins" and "Joseph's earlier children" views arose from a wish to defend Mary's perpetual virginity. He thinks they were most naturally Joseph and Mary's children. (This is a known Protestant–Catholic/Orthodox difference. I could not read the Catholic or Orthodox side directly.) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm

**v. 6**
- The word "only" implies all the other apostles took support. Barnabas probably copied Paul's practice. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm
- Oddly, the Corinthians respected Paul and Barnabas less because they took no pay. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/

**v. 7**
- The soldier, vine-grower and shepherd show the church's practice is ordinary. Ellicott divides Paul's case into three kinds of argument: from what others do (vv. 1–6), from everyday life (v. 7), and from authority (v. 8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm

**v. 8**
- Paul appeals to a principle God gave, not a merely human one. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm

**v. 9**
- Ellicott explains how oxen threshed grain. He says the question does not deny God's care for animals. The law's main purpose was to teach people humanity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm
- Guzik: the principle is that a minister may be supported by the people he serves. He quotes Calvin warning against reading Scripture as allegory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/
- "It is written" stresses the lasting authority of the written Word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-9-commentary

**v. 10**
- Starving those who prepare your food would take away their hope. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/

**v. 11**
- Spiritual work may rightly be repaid with material support. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/
- Matthew Henry argues from fairness: people who receive spiritual blessing shouldn't begrudge their ministers a living. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_009.cfm

**v. 12**
- Paul endured hardship so his enemies could not accuse him of preaching for gain. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm
- Being paid or unpaid didn't matter to Paul. Only the gospel mattered. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/
- The Greek word for "endure" is drawn from "roof," meaning to cover over. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-9-commentary

**vv. 13–14**
- The Lord's command applies to anyone who preaches, not just apostles (compare Matthew 10:10; Luke 10:8). Ministers who take support should work hard for it. Guzik quotes Adam Clarke's sharp attack on idle or greedy ministers. (This is the nearest I found to a warning against money-centred ministry. It does not name prosperity teaching.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/
- Matthew Henry: a minister may give up the right without sin, but people who refuse support break Christ's appointment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_009.cfm

**v. 15**
- Ellicott notes the Greek wording varies. He favours a reading where Paul breaks off mid-sentence and then says "no man shall make it void." The meaning stays the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm
- Paul is not hinting that he wants to be paid. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/

**vv. 16–17**
- Paul had a calling, not "preacher's itch." His boast is preaching without pay, not preaching itself. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/
- One teacher warns that this "necessity" is the call to preach. It does not apply to every believer, or to someone coming to God for salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-9-commentary
- Matthew Henry: only service given willingly can be rewarded. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_009.cfm

**v. 18**
- Ellicott suggests reading it without a question mark. On his view, the "reward" Paul seeks is the Corinthians' good. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm
- Paul set himself apart from religious entrepreneurs of his day. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/
- On merit: Matthew Henry insists that giving up the right does not "supererogate," meaning earn credit beyond duty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_009.cfm The Pulpit Commentary (at v. 27) says Paul's constant effort shows he did not believe in "works of supererogation." This is Protestant wording aimed at the Catholic idea; I couldn't check the Catholic side. https://biblehub.com/1_corinthians/9-27.htm

**v. 19**
- "Win the more" means more than he would have won by using his rights. Ellicott thinks it may also mean more than any other apostle won. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm
- "Slave" here does not mean other people own him. It means he gives up his rights. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-9-commentary

**v. 20**
- Paul kept parts of the ceremonial law to remove Jewish prejudices. (Matthew Henry) Guzik points to Acts 21:23-26. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_009.cfm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/

**v. 21 (meaning of "law of Christ")**
- Calvin (Reformed): the bracketed phrase softens "without law." Christ's teaching lacks nothing as a rule for upright living. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/9-21.html
- Barnes: the verse "would destroy all the refuges of the Antinomians." Freedom in the gospel does not free us from law. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/1-corinthians/9-21.html
- Constable (dispensational): God's law for Jews before the cross was Moses' Law. For Christians today it is the Law of Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/9-21.html
- Jack Arnold: the law of Christ is the law of love, expressed in the moral law of both Testaments. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-9-commentary
- Cole: it means the moral parts of God's law. Paul would eat idol meat but would never use profanity. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-9-commentary
- One commentary quotes Luther: a Christian is a free lord of all and a dutiful servant of all. (This is quoted second-hand. I found no Lutheran-site source.) https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/9-21.html

**v. 22**
- Paul's humility let him hope only to save "some." (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm
- Table Talk (Ligonier): Paul adapted only in matters that don't matter morally, and never compromised doctrine. Gordon Fee (modern scholar) says the passage is about how Paul behaved, not about changing the message. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-9-commentary
- Ligonier warns that people copy Paul's method while ignoring the limit he set in v. 21. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/all-things-to-all-people
- Clarke: Paul adapted to save souls, not to gain money or honour. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-9-commentary

**v. 23**
- Utley: this is a link verse. It does not teach salvation by works. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-9-commentary
- Paul was willing to offend people over the gospel and nothing else. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/for-the-gospels-sake/

**vv. 24–25**
- Giving up rights is the price of competing for an imperishable crown. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-9/
- Constable takes the prize as a reward at Christ's judgment seat. MacArthur calls it Christlikeness in heaven. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-9-commentary
- Believers are not rivals in this race, and we don't run it to get into heaven. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_corinthians_924_commentary

**v. 26**
- Paul made every blow count, like a disciplined boxer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_corinthians_926_commentary

**v. 27 (the main point of dispute)**
- Word meaning: *adokimos* comes from metal that fails a test (Barnes). The Pulpit Commentary pictures a herald who announces the rules and is then disqualified himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/9-27.html
- The body: it is figurative, about subduing appetites, not causing real pain (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary says Paul's way was not self-torture but labour and self-denial for others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/9.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/9-27.htm Clarke: the body must be the soul's slave. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_corinthians_927_commentary
- Wesley (labelled Arminian/Methodist on the page): Paul kept his body under "by all kinds of self denial." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/9-27.html
- Saved but losing reward or usefulness: Gill says Paul feared disgrace in his ministry, not damnation, because a chosen vessel "could not be eternally lost." The Geneva notes say the word contrasts with "approved," not with "elect." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/9-27.htm Leon Morris, Vine, Wuest, Swindoll and others on preceptaustin say the same (no loss of salvation). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_corinthians_927_commentary
- Real danger of being lost: Barnes says Paul felt he might be lost even after all his success. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/9-27.htm The Homilist says personal religion, including persevering struggle, is essential to final salvation. Talmage says ministers may finally be lost. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/9-27.html
- Proving faith was never real: one preceptaustin writer links the word to 2 Corinthians 13:5, meaning Christ was never in the person and the race "was a sham." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_corinthians_927_commentary
- A middle note: a homiletical commentary says safety comes from God's grace, with which a person must co-operate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/9-27.html
